title: Top tennis players end public campaign phase after Grand Slam Advisory Council formation
dek: Top tennis players have halted the public phase of their 18-month campaign for increased prize money from Grand Slams after the four major tournaments announced a new Grand Slam Player Advisory Council. Players reserve the right to restart the campaign if the council fails to deliver on their aims, which include revenue sharing, better representation, health options, and pensions.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: Players requested 22% of Grand Slam tournament revenues; the slams have increased total prize money by $415.6 million since July 2025 but have not yet committed to formal revenue-sharing agreements or reached the 22% figure.
bottom_line: The council's authority, budget, voting structure, and negotiation timeline remain unspecified. If the council produces no formal revenue-sharing agreement within a defined period, players have signaled they will return to public pressure. The September 14, 2026 statement marks a ceasefire, not a settlement.
body: Top tennis players have concluded the public phase of their 18-month campaign for increased prize money from Grand Slams, according to ESPN's reporting. The shift follows the announcement last month by the Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon, and US Open of a new Grand Slam Player Advisory Council.

In a statement reported by ESPN, players said: "The players will now work directly with the Grand Slams to establish the council, through which players themselves will be directly consulted and able to negotiate on an ongoing basis. Now that a formal council exists to carry this work forward, the public phase of the campaign led by the unified group of top players comes to a close."

The campaign, which began with top players including Aryna Sabalenka and Coco Gauff limiting media appearances and threatening a potential boycott of the slams before Paris, sought 22% of tournament revenues. According to ESPN, players also pursued better representation, health options, and pensions.

Formal proposals were submitted on July 31, 2025. Since that date, prize money across the 2025 and 2026 US Open, 2026 Australian Open, Wimbledon, and Roland Garros has grown to $415.6 million in total, per ESPN's reporting. Players estimate that more than $30 million of that increase represents gains above the pre-campaign growth rate.

The Grand Slams, the Australian Open, French Open, and US Open operated by nonprofit governing bodies, and Wimbledon run by the private All England Club, have not yet committed to formal revenue-sharing agreements or reached the players' 22% target. However, according to ESPN's account of the players' statement: "While the Grand Slams have not yet reached this figure or committed to formal revenue sharing agreements, all have increased prize money significantly beyond their long-term trend prior to the campaign, over the past 18 months."
Crucially, players reserve leverage for escalation. ESPN reports the players' statement said: "Players reserve the right to re-start the campaign should the council fail to deliver on these aims."
